concept.name: Tool use
concept.definition: The ability of a language model to invoke external tools — calculators, search engines, databases, trading or market-data APIs — by emitting structured calls whose results are fed back into the model's context. Schick et al.'s Toolformer (2023) showed a model can learn in a self-supervised way which APIs to call, when, and with what arguments.
concept.intuition: Let the model operate the instruments instead of playing every instrument itself: it decides what it needs, calls the tool, and reads the result.
concept.mechanics: Available tools are declared to the model with names, descriptions, and argument schemas; during generation the model emits a call (tool name + JSON arguments), the host system executes it, and the result is appended to the context so generation continues with the real data. Training or prompting teaches when a call is warranted.
concept.failure_modes: Models call wrong tools, pass malformed or hallucinated arguments, misinterpret results, or loop on repeated calls; tools with side effects (orders, emails) turn a model error into a real-world action. Each tool expands the attack surface for prompt injection through returned content.
concept.misconceptions: Tool access does not make the model understand the tool's domain — it can call a market-data API correctly and still misread the response. Restricting the model's text does not restrict what it can do through tools; permissions must be enforced outside the model.
concept.example: Asked for the notional value of 5 ES contracts, an agent calls a market-data tool for the current S&P 500 futures price, then a calculator for price × multiplier × quantity, instead of estimating from memory.

citations.source: Schick et al., 'Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools' (2023)
